Strengtheneth
STRENG-then-eth
v. (3rd pers. sing.)
The third-person singular present of strengthen, from strength, Saxon strengthu. Webster 1828: maketh strong; giveth strength or firmness to; confirmeth. Philippians 4:13 makes it the hinge of one of the most quoted and most misquoted verses in Scripture.

Biblical Definition

Strengtheneth answers the question of where a man’s ability comes from, and Paul’s answer is a Person: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me (Philippians 4:13). The context is not achievement but contentment; Paul has just said he has learned both to be abased and to abound, both to be full and to be hungry, and the all things he can do is the whole range of circumstance he has been given to bear. Ecclesiastes locates a different kind of strength: Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men which are in the city (Ecclesiastes 7:19) — a wise man in a besieged town outweighs ten captains. The psalmist names an ordinary means through which God gives strength, and does not apologise for its ordinariness: bread which strengtheneth man’s heart (Psalm 104:15). And Proverbs describes the virtuous woman in the language of a labourer: She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms (Proverbs 31:17). The picture across these texts is consistent. Strength is given, not generated; it comes through Christ, through wisdom, through bread, and through work, and in every case the receiving is by God’s appointment.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives STRENGTHENETH as the third person singular of STRENGTHEN: to make strong or stronger; to add strength to, whether physical, moral, or intellectual; to confirm; to establish; to animate or encourage.

expand to see more

STRENGTHENETH — the third person singular, present tense, of the verb STRENGTHEN.

STRENGTHEN, v.t. — To make strong or stronger; to add strength to, either physical or moral.

To confirm; to establish; to fix more firmly; as, to strengthen a resolution or an obligation.

To animate; to encourage; to fix in resolution; as, strengthen thy brethren.

From strength, Saxon strengthu, from strang, strong — the root also of string and strong.

Key Scripture

Philippians 4:13 — "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me."

Ecclesiastes 7:19 — "Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men which are in the city."

Psalm 104:15 — "And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man's heart."

Proverbs 31:17 — "She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms."

Modern Corruption

Philippians 4:13 has been detached from its context and made a promise of achievement — printed on athletic gear and quoted before examinations and business ventures — when Paul wrote it about knowing how to be hungry.

expand to see more

Read verses 11 and 12 and the misquotation collapses. I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content… I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. Then comes verse 13. The all things is that list: hunger, abasement, need, and also plenty, which Paul evidently regarded as the harder of the two to survive. The verse promises sufficiency to endure whatever God assigns, not success in whatever a man attempts. Used the popular way it becomes a charm, and it fails the first believer who prayed it over an outcome God had determined otherwise — which is precisely the man Paul wrote it to comfort.

Psalm 104:15 guards a second and quieter error, the false spirituality that is embarrassed by ordinary means. God gives strength through bread. He gives gladness through wine and dignity through oil, and the psalm lists them among His works of providence without a hint of apology. A piety that expects strength only through extraordinary experience and despises sleep, food, work and the company of the saints is not more spiritual than the psalmist; it is less biblical. Proverbs 31:17 makes the same point from the side of labour: the woman strengthens her arms, and Scripture counts that among her praises rather than against them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chazaq (H2388), to be strong, to strengthen, to hold fast; amats (H553), to be alert, to make firm; Greek endunamoo (G1743), to empower, to infuse strength; krataioo (G2901), to make mighty.

expand to see more

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be or make strong, to seize; behind be strong and of a good courage (Joshua 1:9).

Hebrew amats (H553) — to be alert, to be courageous, to make firm; the constant companion of chazaq in the charge to Joshua.

Greek endunamoo (G1743) — to empower from within; Christ which strengtheneth me (Philippians 4:13) and be strong in the Lord (Ephesians 6:10).

Greek krataioo (G2901) — to make mighty; strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man (Ephesians 3:16).

Greek sthenoo (G4599) — to make firm; one of the four verbs of 1 Peter 5:10, where God perfects, stablishes, strengthens and settles His people.

Usage

"I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me (Philippians 4:13) — written about knowing how to be hungry."

"Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men (Ecclesiastes 7:19) — one wise man outweighs ten captains."

"Bread which strengtheneth man’s heart (Psalm 104:15) — God’s strength through ordinary means."
